'''Ian William Murison Smith''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|FRS|FRSC}} (15 June 1937 – 8 November 2016)<ref name=rsbm>{{cite journal|last1=Hancock|first1=Gus|title=Ian William Murison Smith. 15 June 1937—8 November 2016|journal=[[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]]|publisher=[[Royal Society]]|location=London|year=2018|volume=64 |pages=401–419 |issn=0080-4606|doi=10.1098/rsbm.2017.0033|url=https://www.birmingham.ac.uk/Documents/college-eps/chemistry/news/royal-society-biographical-memoir-ian-smith.pdf|doi-access=free}} {{free access}}</ref><ref name=whoswho>{{Who's Who | type=was|author=Anon| title=Smith, Prof. Ian William Murison | id = U35371 | year = 2007 | doi = 10.1093/ww/9780199540884.013.35371| edition = online [[Oxford University Press]]|location=Oxford}}</ref> was a chemist who served as a [[research fellow]] and [[lecturer]] in the [[Department of Chemistry, University of Cambridge]] from 1963 to 1985 and [[Professor of Chemistry]] at the [[University of Birmingham]] from 1985 to 2002.<ref name=whoswho/><ref name=cam>{{cite web|title=Professor Ian Murison Smith, FRS|publisher=University of Cambridge|website=ch.cam.ac.uk|url=https://www.ch.cam.ac.uk/news/professor-ian-murison-smith-frs|author=Anon|year=2016}}</ref>

==Education==
Smith was educated at [[Giggleswick School]]<ref name=whoswho/> then in the [[West Riding of Yorkshire]] and the [[University of Cambridge]] where he studied the [[Natural Sciences Tripos]] as an undergraduate student of [[Christ's College, Cambridge]].<ref name=rsbm/> He graduated in 1960 and went on to gain a [[PhD]] in 1964 supervised by Tony Callear.<ref name=rsbm/>

==Research and career==
Smith was a leading researcher in [[reaction kinetics]], [[energy transfer]] and [[molecular dynamics]] in [[gas phase]] systems.<ref name=rsbm/> He was elected a [[List of Fellows of the Royal Society elected in 1995|Fellow of the Royal Society (FRS) in 1995]],<ref name=rsbm/> a [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry]] (FRSC){{when|date=February 2018}} and awarded the [[Tilden Prize]] in 1983<ref name=rsbm/> and the [[Polanyi Medal]] in 1990 by the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]]. His former doctoral students include [[David Klenerman]]<ref name=klenesweep>{{cite web|title=Interdisciplinary Award 2007 Winner|url=http://www.rsc.org/ScienceAndTechnology/Awards/InterdisciplinaryPrize/2007winner1.asp|publisher=[[Royal Society of Chemistry]]|access-date=2016-01-26}}</ref><ref name=kphd>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|publisher=University of Cambridge|url=http://idiscover.lib.cam.ac.uk/primo-explore/fulldisplay?docid=44CAM_ALMA21428177930003606&context=L&vid=44CAM_PROD&search_scope=SCOP_CAM_ALL&tab=cam_lib_coll&lang=en_US|title=Infrared chemiluminescence using a SISAM spectrometer|first= David|last=Klenerman|date=1985|id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.355881}}|website=lib.cam.ac.uk|oclc=499899771}}</ref> and Gus Hancock.<ref name=rsbm/><ref name=guscv>{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180216160228/http://infiqc.fcq.unc.edu.ar/repositorio/CV_Hancock%20.pdf|archive-date=2018-02-16|url=http://infiqc.fcq.unc.edu.ar/repositorio/CV_Hancock%20.pdf|website=infiqc.fcq.unc.edu.ar|title=Professor Gus (Graham) Hancock BA(Dublin) MA(Dublin, Oxon) PhD(Cantab) Curriculum Vitae}}</ref><ref name=hancock>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|publisher=University of Cambridge|url=https://idiscover.lib.cam.ac.uk/primo-explore/fulldisplay?docid=44CAM_ALMA21429670020003606&context=L&vid=44CAM_PROD&search_scope=SCOP_CAM_ALL&tab=cam_lib_coll&lang=en_US|title=A study of some elementary processes using infrared chemiluminescence|first= (Graham) Gus|last=Hancock|date=1971|id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.458050}}|website=lib.cam.ac.uk|oclc=500462959}}</ref>

==Personal life==
He married Sue Morrish in 1961. They had four children.<ref name=rsbm/>
